title: Deterministic Verification and a Single-Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics we generated one candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if failing, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251. Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair. We explicitly disclose that the preregistered sim‑to‑real contrast was not executed and that the confirmatory estimand executed here is the paired guarded−baseline difference on the synthetic/emulation partition. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being explored as intent-to-configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), promising faster authoring of device CLI sequences and intent-driven automation. Stochastic generation however creates operational risk: syntax errors, incorrect command ordering, local-policy violations, and vendor-CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or non-functional device changes. Prior empirical and survey work documents LLM feasibility for draft configurations while highlighting the continuing need for deterministic verification or human oversight [1],[2].

A widely adopted architectural response is to interpose a deterministic validator between generation and acceptance, optionally followed by bounded automated repair — a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pattern — which accepts only validator-passed candidates or attempts limited repair when mechanically verifiable defects are detected [3],[4]. These pipelines demonstrably reduce mechanically verifiable error classes (syntax, simple ordering and local-policy violations), but open questions remain about the marginal benefit of such guardrails when modern LLM outputs already conform to validator encodings under constrained task regimes.

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment that isolates the marginal verifier+single-repair effect when the same initial candidate is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). By design the experiment measures only the validator-and-repair marginal effect on identical model outputs rather than conflating generation variability across conditions. We executed N_pairs = 250 intents on a synthetic/emulation partition; results, execution accounting, representative artifacts, and analysis logs are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement. Our principal contribution is the concrete, artifact-grounded quantification of the marginal verifier-detected improvement (and its statistical bounds) under shared_initial_candidate semantics for a constrained NetOps task set.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and benchmarks in the NetOps and LLM literature motivate generate–verify architectures and evaluation practices. Representative empirical and survey studies show (a) LLMs can produce usable draft configurations under controlled conditions [1],[2]; (b) deterministic verification tools and header-space / model-checking techniques provide mechanized checks for forwarding, reachability, and many local-policy properties and are commonly used as validators in GVR pipelines [3],[5]; and (c) generate-and-verify and program-repair workflows increase the detection and correction rate for mechanically checkable defects in code and configuration domains, with limitations for deeper semantic correctness and cross-vendor subtleties [4],[6]. Security analyses of prompt-injection and retrieval-based threats emphasize the need for filtering and validation layers in LLM-integrated pipelines but note that adaptive adversaries remain an unresolved operational threat [7].

This work differs from prior reports by (i) using a preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics that isolates the validator/repair marginal effect on identical generated candidates, (ii) reporting complete provider-call accounting and deterministic reconciliation for stage-level modeling of generation and repair calls, and (iii) archiving comprehensive validator traces and reconciliation artifacts so that the exact numeric outcomes and stage mappings are auditable.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration, estimand, and design. The experiment was preregistered as study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 and specified a confirmatory paired design with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration froze the single-repair policy, exclusion rules, analysis tests (exact McNemar two-sided and paired bootstrap percentile CI), and the maximum model-call budget. The preregistration artifact and full manifest are archived in the public evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics (explicit). Under the registered shared_initial_candidate design exactly one initial model-generation call was produced per intent and that same generated candidate was reused for both episodes (baseline and guarded). No independent first-pass generation per condition was performed. This design isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validation and the single permitted repair on an identical candidate. Provider-call accounting and deterministic reconciliation that demonstrate the mapping from generation and repair stages to completed episodes are available in the archived reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) and in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json); those artifacts contain stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1} and hosted_model_call_event_count = 251, which reconcile to the 500 completed episodes produced from the 250 shared candidates plus the single permitted repair call.

Task generation and task payloads. A deterministic task generator produced 250 constrained intent tasks (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task payload encoded: initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). Tasks exercised workflow constraints (e.g., make-before-break uplink switchover, paired-link atomic MTU changes, safe access transfer patterns) and enforced protected interfaces that must not be modified. Representative task payloads and the full task manifest are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and include explicit workflow_policies used by the deterministic validator.

Model and invocation policy. The declared model used for all initial generations was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). For each intent we executed one shared initial generation call (the shared candidate). The preregistration allowed up to one automated repair call per episode; the execution used that policy permissively but only one repair call was exercised in the run. The provider recorded stage-level events and the adapter audit reconciles stage_counts and hosted_model_call totals (see analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Guarded pipeline and deterministic validator. The guarded pipeline submitted the shared candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5, which implements full_intent_constraint_validation: parsing CLI sequences, counting parsed_command_count, checking required_sequence ordering, validating workflow constraints (e.g., group-activity constraints), and comparing the resulting final_state snapshot to the expected_final_state encoded in the task payload. Validator outputs include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes (if any), and a boolean valid flag. When the validator returned valid = false for a guarded episode, the pipeline permitted up to one automated, template-driven repair attempt (preregistered repair templates only) and re-submitted the repaired candidate to the validator. Repair templates were constrained to syntactic and ordering fixes; no free-form multi-iteration repair or human-in-the-loop escalation was allowed by design.

Inclusion/Exclusion, contamination, and missingness rules. The preregistered exclusion rules removed items failing deterministic vendor-parsers that prevented verification, or items with detected credential-like tokens or denylist hits. The contamination detectors flagged instruction-like embedded tokens or private-address artifacts; flagged items would be excluded from the primary analysis and treated in sensitivity analyses. In this confirmatory run no episodes were excluded or flagged: complete_pair_count = 250 and the contamination summary is empty for the confirmatory partition (analysis/contamination_summary.csv).

Confirmatory analysis executor. The preregistered primary analysis used a paired binary procedure implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1. The primary test is an exact (two-sided) McNemar test on the paired outcomes; we also computed a paired-bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the guarded − baseline paired difference using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The analysis artifacts and contingency table are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv).
sections.results:
Execution and raw counts. Execution completed the preregistered confirmatory partition with planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, complete_pair_count = 250, and model_calls_used = 251. The model-call accounting reconciles to 250 shared initial_generation calls plus 1 repair call (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 251 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}).

Primary binary outcomes and contingency. Validator-scored successes: baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table observed is n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The single discordant pair (baseline failed, guarded passed) corresponds to the only exercised repair call; the repair-conversion rate on the confirmatory partition is 1/250 = 0.004 (0.4%).

Statistical inference and uncertainty. The exact McNemar two-sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the guarded − baseline paired difference (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (i.e., 0 – 1.2 percentage points). These numeric analysis outputs and the bootstrap parameters are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.

Representative validator diagnostics. Validator traces for passed episodes include parsed_command_count and required_command_count fields equal to the number of commands needed by the required_sequence in the task payload. For example, a hard-difficulty task (task-000003) had parsed_command_count = 6 and required_command_count = 6 and a valid = true verdict in both baseline and guarded episodes (see execution/scoring/task-000003-baseline.json and -guarded.json). Representative raw responses and normalized configurations for sample tasks are archived in execution/responses and execution/scoring entries (sha256-summarized in the evidence bundle).

Repair exercise and conversion. Only one automated repair call occurred (stage_counts: repair = 1). That repair converted the sole failing baseline candidate into a guarded-pass; the repair trace and the guarded scoring artifact for that pair are archived (execution/scoring/task-000XYZ-guarded.json and the corresponding repair_provider_trace in the raw results manifest). No other repairs were needed for the confirmatory partition.

Missingness and exclusions. No episodes were excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis: analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 250 and all other missingness counts = 0. Contamination detectors flagged no confirmatory episodes, so no preregistered sensitivity exclusion was required for the confirmatory estimand.
sections.discussion:
Operational meaning of the observed near‑null marginal effect. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the constrained synthetic/emulation partition used here, the marginal verifier-detected benefit of inserting a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair was small: initial gpt-5-mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the guarded pipeline converted the lone failing candidate via the single permitted repair. The paired-bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) provides an empirical bound on the possible verifier-improvement under this pipeline and task scope.

Why the verifier improvement was small (artifact-grounded factors). Three artifact-grounded factors explain the small observed guarded gain: (1) the deterministic task generator encoded constrained intents and allowed_touched_fields and required_sequences that reduced task ambiguity and favored well-formed CLI sequences (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries); (2) the declared model (gpt-5-mini) produced highly consistent, syntactically well-formed sequences for these constrained intents; and (3) the deterministic validator checks mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, expected_final_state snapshots) and does not capture broader behavioral correctness in live protocol execution or cross-device emergent interactions.

Power, preregistration assumptions, and interpretation. The preregistration power calculation assumed a baseline pass rate ≈ 0.90 when selecting N_pairs = 250 to target detection of a 15 percentage-point absolute effect with ≈80% power. The realized baseline pass rate (0.996) is substantially higher than assumed and therefore reduces the ability to reject a null of zero paired difference for small absolute improvements. Consequently, the most practically informative output is the paired-bootstrap confidence interval that bounds the maximum plausible verifier-detected improvement under the study conditions rather than the p-value alone. Readers should interpret the reported CI and exact counts as concrete performance bounds for this model, task bank, validator, and single-repair policy.

Threats to validity and scope. Internal validity: results depend on prompt templates, single-repair policy, shared_initial_candidate semantics, and the precise validator encoding. Construct validity: the deterministic validator measures mechanically verifiable correctness (syntax, required_sequence, final_state snapshot) but does not assert live protocol-level correctness. External validity: the confirmatory evidence covers only the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed in this run. Security: adaptive prompt-injection and retrieval-based adversaries were not exercised; adversarial robustness remains an open question.

Implications and appropriate operational framing. These results show that in tightly constrained emulation-style tasks with a capable LLM the marginal verifier-detected improvement from a single repair may be small. This should not be interpreted to mean that validators or repair stages are unnecessary in broader or adversarial operational contexts: (a) validator scope matters — validators that check properties not present here (e.g., live forwarding invariants across vendor-specific implementations) could catch errors not exercised in our task bank; (b) multi-iteration repairs, human escalation, or richer external tests could produce different operational benefits; and (c) production heterogeneity and adversaries may materially change the benefit calculus. Future work should evaluate the preregistered production-like partition and adversarial scenarios to generalize findings.

Reproducibility and auditability. All run artifacts (raw model responses, execution manifest, validator traces, repair traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis outputs) are archived in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement. Key numeric reconciliation facts reported above (model_calls_used = 251, stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}, contingency counts n11=249/n10=1/n01=0/n00=0, and bootstrap parameters) are directly reproducible from the archived manifests and analysis CSVs (e.g., analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv).
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier-detected marginal benefit of deterministic validation plus one permitted automated repair on identical LLM-generated configuration candidates. In N = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the single permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; p = 1.0). We explicitly disclose that the preregistered sim‑to‑real confirmatory contrast was not executed and that the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on the synthetic/emulation partition only. Broader production, adversarial, multi-model, and multi-iteration repair evaluations remain necessary to establish generality. All execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this paper are archived and available in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: After an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer-review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and performed pre-lock infrastructure development only; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Models, tools, and framework: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode as specified in the preregistration. Execution manifest recorded planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, and model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) as reconciled by the adapter audit (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution/execution_manifest.json in the evidence bundle).

Preregistration and immutable prompt references (archived): preregistration study id = study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1. Immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Key execution artifacts used for reconciliation and numeric reporting include execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json (all archived together in the evidence bundle referenced by the submission). The evidence bundle contains the full execution and analysis manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and artifact hashes referenced in this manuscript.

Executed confirmatory estimand and deviation disclosure: The preregistration included multiple partitions (synthetic/emulation, community, production-like) and a preregistered sim-to-real confirmatory contrast. Deviation disclosure (explicit): the preregistered sim-to-real confirmatory comparison was not executed in this run; the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated on the synthetic/emulation partition only (N_pairs = 250; shared_initial_candidate semantics). Provider-call accounting in the archive reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) and stage_counts {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}, consistent with the shared_initial_candidate design. Full execution and analysis manifests and per-artifact hashes are archived and referenced in the evidence bundle.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed and remain exploratory.

Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) but did not measure broader semantic or behavioral correctness (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions).
Single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repairs or human-in-the-loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval-based attacks (adaptive prompt-injection, vendor-targeted exploit vectors) and large-scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
